blocks.text: SCI damages the spinal cord, interrupting movement, sensation and autonomic control below the level of injury. Causes include trauma (road accidents, falls, gunshot) and non-traumatic causes (tumour, infection, disc, vascular). **Tetraplegia** affects arms, trunk and legs (cervical injury); **paraplegia** affects trunk and legs (thoracic, lumbar, sacral injury).
The injury is classified using the International Standards for Neurological Classification of SCI (ISNCSCI), including the **ASIA Impairment Scale (AIS)**:

rows: Complete: no sensory or motor function in the lowest sacral segments (S4 to S5)
Sensory incomplete: sensation but no motor function below the level, including S4 to S5
Motor incomplete: motor function below the level; more than half of key muscles below the level have strength below grade 3
Motor incomplete: at least half of key muscles below the level are grade 3 or more

sections.title: B. Functional expectations by level (approximate, complete injuries) [Ref – to verify]

rows: Power wheelchair with head or chin control; may need ventilation support
Power chair; manual chair with adaptations on flat surfaces; assisted feeding with aids
Tenodesis grip; manual chair; independent transfers possible with a board
Standing or walking with orthoses for exercise
Community walking with aids and orthoses possible

sections.title: C. Ask the right questions and review

blocks.text: Level and AIS grade, spinal stability and orthosis orders (collar, brace), surgery, respiratory status, bladder and bowel program, skin, pain (neuropathic), autonomic symptoms, home and social situation, goals.

items: Respiratory: vital capacity, cough strength (peak cough flow), breathing pattern.
ISNCSCI motor and sensory examination (key muscles and key sensory points, C2 to S4-5).
Tone, spasms, range (especially hamstrings, ankles, shoulders).
Function: rolling, sitting balance, transfers, wheelchair skills, standing, walking for incomplete injuries.

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Sudden pounding headache, high BP, flushing and sweating above the injury, slow heart rate (injury at T6 or above)
Sit the patient up, lower legs, loosen tight clothing and straps, check bladder (catheter kinked or full bladder) and bowel, monitor BP, call medical help
Recline, raise legs; use binder and stockings; progress slowly
Redness that does not fade after pressure is removed
New loss of function above the level

blocks.label: STOP AND THINK
body: Autonomic dysreflexia is a medical emergency. A triggering stimulus below the injury (most often a full bladder) causes a dangerous rise in blood pressure. Act fast and find the trigger.

steps: **Acute:** spinal precautions, respiratory care, positioning, passive range, prevention of complications.
**Spine stable and medically cleared:** sitting tolerance, tilt table, balance.
**Set goals based on level and AIS grade.**
**Train** functional skills: rolling, transfers, wheelchair skills; walking practice for motor incomplete injuries.

rows: Breathing exercises, assisted cough (manual pressure under the diaphragm timed with the patient's cough), inspiratory muscle training, abdominal binder

Daily stretching; keep hamstrings long enough (about 100 to 110 degrees straight-leg raise) for long sitting and dressing [Ref – to verify]; in C6 injuries preserve tenodesis: do not stretch finger flexors with the wrist extended
Shoulder depressors, triceps, latissimus dorsi, all preserved muscles; progressive resistance
Rolling, lying to long sitting, sliding board transfers, depression lifts, wheelchair propulsion and wheelie skills, floor-to-chair transfers
Overground training, treadmill with body-weight support, orthoses, FES
Pressure relief every 15 to 30 minutes in sitting (lean forward or sideways) [Ref – to verify]

blocks.text: FES cycling and FES-assisted walking in selected patients; standing frames for weight-bearing and wellbeing.
ISNCSCI, Spinal Cord Independence Measure (SCIM), walking measures (10MWT, WISCI II), respiratory measures.

items: **Patient with C6 complete injury: what grasp can be trained?** Tenodesis grasp: active wrist extension passively closes the fingers.
**Why not stretch finger flexors with the wrist extended in C6 injury?** It would lengthen them and lose the tenodesis effect.
**A T4 patient becomes flushed with a severe headache and BP 190/110. Action?** Autonomic dysreflexia: sit up, loosen clothing, check bladder and catheter, call medical help.
**What does AIS C mean?** Motor incomplete with most key muscles below the level weaker than grade 3.
**Why maintain hamstring length?** To allow long sitting for dressing and transfers.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Explain ISNCSCI and the AIS grades.
Plan respiratory, skin and functional rehabilitation.
